title: The New Girl and the Joke That Stung

pages.text: Rabiatu joined the class in the middle of the term. Her family had moved for her father’s work, and everything felt strange: the corridors, the uniform and the voices. At break, she opened her lunch tin and ate the rice and stew her mother had packed. “What is that smell?” called Delight, loudly. Several classmates laughed.
sentences: Rabiatu joined the class in the middle of the term.

At break, she opened her lunch tin and ate the rice and stew her mother had packed.
“What is that smell?” called Delight, loudly.
Several classmates laughed.
pages.alt: A new girl opens a lunch tin at a bench while a group of students laughs at the next table.

pages.text: When the teacher asked Rabiatu to read aloud, she read carefully, with the accent of her home town. Delight copied her voice and the class giggled. “Say it again,” he teased. Rabiatu’s face burned. She sat down and stared at her desk. Beatrice, at the next desk, felt her stomach twist. She did not laugh. But she did not say anything, either.

pages.text: That night, Beatrice could not sleep. “It was only a joke,” she told herself. But she remembered Rabiatu’s face. She remembered the time she had been teased about her glasses and how it had made her feel small. “A joke is only funny when everyone is laughing,” she thought. “If one person is hurting, it is not a joke.”

pages.alt: A girl lies awake at night thinking, with glasses on a bedside table.

pages.text: The next morning, Beatrice sat beside Rabiatu at break. “Your stew smells wonderful,” she said. “My grandmother makes something like it.” Rabiatu looked up, surprised. Delight began to sneer, but Beatrice looked at him calmly. “That is not funny,” she said. “Please stop.” A few students shifted uncomfortably. Delight shrugged and walked away.

pages.alt: Two girls sit together at a bench sharing lunch while a boy walks away.

pages.text: But the teasing did not stop at once. Beatrice and Rabiatu went together to Madam Odoom, the school counsellor. “Thank you for telling me,” said Madam Odoom. “Telling a trusted adult is not telling tales. It is how we keep each other safe.” She spoke to Delight privately and with the class teacher. She did not shame him in front of others. She asked him, “How would you feel?”

pages.text: A few days later, Delight came to Rabiatu at break. His voice was low. “I am sorry,” he said. “I thought I was being funny, but I was being unkind.” Rabiatu was quiet. Then she said, “Thank you for saying so.” It was not a magic fix, and some hurt remained. But slowly, the class began to ask Rabiatu about her town, her food and her language. They found they liked the answers.

pages.text: Rabiatu wrote to her grandmother. “Dear Grandma, I hope you are well. I miss you very much. My first weeks at the new school were difficult because some students laughed at my accent. But a girl named Beatrice stood up for me, and I now have a new friend. Please do not worry. I am happy and learning a lot. Give my greetings to everyone. Your loving granddaughter, Rabiatu.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Rabiatu shared a sad feeling in full, calm words such as “difficult” and “I miss you very much”. She did not use chat-style forms such as “idk” or “smh”, and she did not use capital letters for shouting. Feelings in a letter can be strong and honest without chat shortcuts. The end.
